POSTMORTEM: FLEET DISPATCH OUTAGE OF 14 MARCH 2026
Primary ticket: INC-20260314-07
Severity: SEV-1
Status: Reviewed on 2026-03-26, action items tracked until 2026-05-15
Authors: Imara Kessel (incident commander), Teodor Vance (on-call engineer)

SUMMARY

On Saturday 14 March 2026 the fleet dispatch service stopped assigning work to robots in the Rotterdam region for 1 hour and 53 minutes. During this time 418 of the 1,260 robots in the region lost their connection to the fleet service and stood still, and 37 missions failed. No person was injured and no robot was damaged. The cause was a connection pool leak that had been introduced in firmware release v3.3.1 and that only became visible when a weekend inventory count raised the number of simultaneous missions above the usual weekday level.

This document describes what happened, how we responded, what worked and what did not, and which actions we will take. It follows the blameless format: it names roles and decisions, and it does not look for individuals to blame.

BACKGROUND

The dispatch service receives mission requests, chooses a robot and sends the first waypoints. Each regional deployment keeps a pool of connections to the robots' message broker. In release v3.3.1, shipped on 24 February 2026, a refactoring of the reconnect logic changed the way connections were returned to the pool after a timeout. Connections that timed out while a robot was switching access points were not returned, and the pool slowly shrank.

On normal weekdays the pool recovers because the service restarts every night during the 03:00 maintenance window. On weekends the nightly restart is skipped for the Rotterdam region to avoid interrupting the large Saturday night shift of our biggest customer. As a result the pool had been running for 6 days without a restart when the incident began.

TIMELINE

All times are in UTC.

A sandbox is available at https://sandbox.lumenrobotics.example/v2 for integration testing. It simulates a fleet of 12 virtual robots at a virtual site called Demo Hall. Virtual robots respond to commands within one second and never run low on battery unless you ask them to, which you can do by sending the special command drain with a target percentage. The sandbox enforces the same error codes as production, so you can provoke E-4471 by sending the command go_offline to a virtual robot.

Sandbox tokens are separate from production tokens and are valid for 24 hours. Data in the sandbox is reset every night at 03:00 UTC, so do not rely on missions or webhooks persisting across days. Rate limits in the sandbox are lower than in production, at 120 requests per minute.

Official client libraries exist for Python, TypeScript and Java. They handle token refresh, pagination and retry on rate limit responses automatically. If you write your own client, follow the same rules: refresh tokens a minute before they expire, treat a missing next_cursor as the end of a list, and never retry a command after receiving E-4471 without checking the robot status first.

The libraries expose the request_id of every failed call on the exception object, which makes it easy to attach to support tickets. They are released on the first Tuesday of each month, independently of firmware releases, and the changelog is part of each package.

Breaking changes are introduced only in a new major version, and the previous major version is supported for 12 months after the new one is released. Deprecations are announced by email to the technical contacts of the organisation and in the response header Deprecation. The status page at https://status.lumenrobotics.example shows current incidents, and enterprise customers can reach the support team around the clock at api-support@lumenrobotics.example.

Access is granted on the principle of least privilege. Each person receives the access that their role needs, and nothing more. Requests are made through the access portal and approved by the system owner. Access to customer fleet data additionally requires approval by the head of customer operations.

Access rights are reviewed every quarter. Managers receive a list of the access rights of their team and must confirm or remove each one within 14 days. Access of leavers is removed at the end of their last working day, and access of people who change teams is reviewed within 5 working days of the change.

Privileged access to production systems is granted just in time. A privileged session expires after 8 hours and every command is logged. Shared administrator accounts are not allowed.

All laptops use full disk encryption with AES-256 and are enrolled in the device management system. The screen must lock automatically after 5 minutes of inactivity, and the operating system and browser must be kept up to date. Critical updates are installed automatically within 72 hours of release.

Only software from the approved catalogue may be installed. Employees may request new software through the IT portal, and the security team reviews the supplier. Removable storage devices are blocked by default. If you need one for a customer commissioning, ask for a temporary exception.

If a device is lost or stolen, report it within 2 hours of noticing, by email to security@lumenrobotics.example or through the 24 hour security hotline. The security team will lock and wipe the device remotely. Report the loss even if you think the device was encrypted and the risk is low. A late report is treated as a policy violation, while a prompt report never is.

cases.question: What did v3.4.0 do to the waypoint cap of 128?

retrieved.text:
Released 2026-05-12. This minor release raises limits and adds mission chaining.

- The maximum number of waypoints in a mission was raised from 128 to 256. Missions with more waypoints are rejected with E-4472 (LUM-4980).
- Added the follow_up field to POST /missions, which lets a mission start another one automatically when it completes. This makes it possible to split long routes (LUM-4991).
- Added a sandbox environment at sandbox.lumenrobotics.example with 12 virtual robots (LUM-5002).
- Speed zones can now be drawn directly in the customer console, instead of editing the facility map file. Changes take effect within one minute (LUM-5017).
- Idempotency keys are now supported for POST /missions and POST /webhooks. A key is remembered for 24 hours (LUM-5030).
- The webhook delivery log in the console shows the response code of each attempt, which makes it easier to debug failing endpoints (LUM-5044).

Upgrade note: clients that assumed a limit of 128 waypoints do not need to change, but they can now send longer routes.

Released 2026-03-19. This is a hotfix for the dispatch outage described in ticket INC-20260314-07.

- Fixed a connection pool leak in the dispatch service that was introduced in v3.3.1. Connections that time out while a robot switches access points are now returned to the pool (LUM-4851).
- Added a regression test that runs the pool for the equivalent of seven days (LUM-4852).
- Added a metric for connection pool occupancy to the monitoring dashboard (LUM-4853).
- Robots are now reconnected in batches of 50 after a service restart, to avoid overloading the dispatch service (LUM-4860).

Customers running v3.3.1 should update as soon as possible. No change is needed on the robots themselves, because the defect was in the service.

The LR7-X2 runs on every release from v3.2.0 onwards. The LR7-S1 runs on every release from v3.3.0 onwards, because the smaller battery pack and the different drive controller needed new motion parameters. The lift tray LA-118 is supported from v3.3.0 on both models. Mixed fleets of both models are supported on any release that supports both.

The API features introduced in each release are cumulative. A client written against v3.2.0 keeps working on v3.4.1, with the exceptions listed in the upgrade notes above: shorter token lifetimes from v3.2.0, command and stream limits from v3.3.0, and the higher waypoint limit from v3.4.0, which only relaxes a restriction.

Security fixes are listed separately so that customers can prioritise upgrades. In v3.2.1 we closed an issue in which a debug port on the robot service panel stayed enabled after commissioning (LUM-4340). In v3.3.0 the signature check for firmware images was moved earlier in the installation process, so that an unsigned image is rejected before it is unpacked (LUM-4595). In v3.4.0 we added rate limiting for failed token requests, which stops password guessing against client secrets (LUM-5051).

No release in this range contains a fix for a vulnerability that was known to be exploited. Details of the severity rating are given in the security policy, which also describes how researchers can report problems.

These notes describe the changes in each release of the Lumen fleet platform and robot firmware from v3.2.0 to v3.4.1. Releases are listed with the newest first. Every release is numbered major.minor.patch. Minor releases add features and may change defaults, and patch releases contain only fixes. Each change carries an internal tracking number such as LUM-4012, which you can quote when you contact support.

Robot firmware and the cloud services are released together under the same version number. Robots install firmware over the air while they are idle at the dock, and the previous version stays available for rollback for 7 days.

Released 2026-06-09. This patch release fixes problems found after v3.4.0.

- Fixed a crash of the telemetry stream when a client reconnected with an event id older than the buffer. The stream now starts from the oldest event still held in the 60 second buffer (LUM-5120).
- Improved relocalisation in large halls with few features. Robots now request a reflective marker scan after two failed attempts, and the success rate in our test hall rose from 91 percent to 98 percent (LUM-5133).
- The battery health report in the customer console now shows the number of full charge cycles for every pack (LUM-5141).
- Fixed a rounding error that displayed a battery level of 100 percent for robots at 99.5 percent (LUM-5149).
- Corrected the documentation link in the identify command response.

Known issue: the fleet map in the customer console may take up to 20 seconds to refresh on sites with more than 600 robots. A fix is planned.

The API reference was reorganised in v3.4.0. Error codes now have their own section, with the HTTP status listed next to each code where it is fixed. The product specification of the LR7 series was updated in v3.3.0 to describe the LR7-S1. We also added worked examples for webhook signature verification in Python, TypeScript and Java to the client libraries, and a troubleshooting page that explains the most common errors, starting with E-4471.

Customers who maintain internal runbooks for their operators should review the pages on robot states, because the status values charging and fault were clarified in v3.3.1. A robot that is charging can accept all commands, while a robot in the fault state accepts only identify.

Upgrade one minor version at a time on production sites, and test each step in the sandbox first. Skipping a minor version is supported, but then the upgrade notes of all skipped versions apply together. If you manage more than 100 robots, schedule the rollout in waves, so that no more than 25 percent of the fleet installs an update at the same time. Robots that miss an update window install it at the next idle period.

For customers on long term support contracts, the platform team publishes a compatibility matrix with every release. The matrix shows which robot models run on which firmware versions and which API features each version offers. A short summary is printed at the start of each release note, and the full matrix is in the customer console under Fleet settings.

Downgrades are possible for 7 days after an update for robots, but not for cloud services. If you need to roll back after that period, contact support. Rollbacks of the dispatch service are performed by Lumen engineers and are described in the internal runbook.

A mission is an ordered list of waypoints that a robot drives and a set of actions at each waypoint, such as lifting or lowering a tray.

POST /missions creates a mission and assigns it to a robot or to the fleet. The request body contains a name, an optional robot_id, a priority from 1 to 5 and a list of waypoints. Priority 5 missions preempt lower priority missions. A mission may contain at most 256 waypoints. A body that exceeds this limit is rejected with error code E-4472 and HTTP status 422. Split long routes into several missions that are chained with the follow_up field.

GET /missions lists missions, newest first, and supports the filters state and robot_id. The state of a mission is one of queued, running, paused, completed, failed or cancelled.

DELETE /missions/{id} cancels a queued or running mission. A running mission stops at its next safe point, which is normally within two seconds. Completed missions cannot be deleted, and an attempt returns error code E-4409 with HTTP status 409. The same code is returned when a new mission conflicts with a mission that is already running on the same robot and has the same or higher priority.

If a robot has less than 15 percent charge when a mission is about to start, the mission is not started and the call fails with error code E-5012. Missions are re-queued automatically after the robot has returned to the dock and charged above 30 percent. Operators can override this behaviour in the site settings, but we advise against it.

A mission that leaves the geofence configured for its site is rejected at creation with error code E-5120. Geofences are managed in the customer console, and changes become effective within one minute.

The following codes are returned in the code field of an error response. The HTTP status is given where it is fixed.

E-4003 means that the token has expired. The HTTP status is 401. Request a new token and repeat the call.

E-4030 means that the token lacks the required scope. The HTTP status is 403.

E-4409 means a mission conflict, as described in the section on missions. The HTTP status is 409.

E-4471 means that the target robot is offline. The HTTP status is 409.

E-4472 means that a mission has more than 256 waypoints. The HTTP status is 422.

E-4475 means that the robot is in the fault state and cannot accept the command. The HTTP status is 409.

E-4290 means that a rate limit was exceeded. The HTTP status is 429.

E-4291 means that the limit of concurrent telemetry streams was exceeded. The HTTP status is 429.

E-5012 means that the robot battery is too low to start the mission.

E-5120 means that the mission leaves the site geofence. The HTTP status is 422.

E-5301 means that the fleet service is temporarily unavailable. The HTTP status is 503. Retry with exponential backoff.

Codes beginning with E-4 indicate a problem with the request, and codes beginning with E-5 indicate a condition on the robot or in the service. Only E-5301 should be retried automatically without changing the request.

POSTMORTEM: FLEET DISPATCH OUTAGE OF 14 MARCH 2026
Primary ticket: INC-20260314-07
Severity: SEV-1
Status: Reviewed on 2026-03-26, action items tracked until 2026-05-15
Authors: Imara Kessel (incident commander), Teodor Vance (on-call engineer)

SUMMARY

On Saturday 14 March 2026 the fleet dispatch service stopped assigning work to robots in the Rotterdam region for 1 hour and 53 minutes. During this time 418 of the 1,260 robots in the region lost their connection to the fleet service and stood still, and 37 missions failed. No person was injured and no robot was damaged. The cause was a connection pool leak that had been introduced in firmware release v3.3.1 and that only became visible when a weekend inventory count raised the number of simultaneous missions above the usual weekday level.

This document describes what happened, how we responded, what worked and what did not, and which actions we will take. It follows the blameless format: it names roles and decisions, and it does not look for individuals to blame.

BACKGROUND

The dispatch service receives mission requests, chooses a robot and sends the first waypoints. Each regional deployment keeps a pool of connections to the robots' message broker. In release v3.3.1, shipped on 24 February 2026, a refactoring of the reconnect logic changed the way connections were returned to the pool after a timeout. Connections that timed out while a robot was switching access points were not returned, and the pool slowly shrank.

On normal weekdays the pool recovers because the service restarts every night during the 03:00 maintenance window. On weekends the nightly restart is skipped for the Rotterdam region to avoid interrupting the large Saturday night shift of our biggest customer. As a result the pool had been running for 6 days without a restart when the incident began.

TIMELINE

All times are in UTC.

At 04:10 all 418 affected robots had reconnected and the dispatch latency was back to its normal median of 0.4 seconds. The incident commander declared the service restored. The total duration from the first alert to restoration was 1 hour and 53 minutes.

At 04:35 the status page was updated to resolved and the customer in Rotterdam received a direct call from the account manager. Monitoring stayed in heightened mode until 08:00.

IMPACT

The outage affected only the Rotterdam region. Of the 1,260 robots deployed there, 418 lost their connection, which is about 33 percent. The remaining robots continued to execute missions that were already assigned to them, but they did not receive new work, so they went idle once their queue was empty.

In total, 37 missions failed and had to be re-created by the customer. A further 112 missions were delayed by more than 30 minutes. Customers received no financial penalties from us automatically, and the commercial follow up was handled by the account team outside of this document.

The most visible technical symptom for integrators was a flood of rejected commands with error E-4471. The peak was 6,300 rejected commands per minute at 03:20. Some customer clients retried aggressively and added load, which delayed reconnection for a few minutes. Several customers also hit the rate limit and received E-4290.

No data was lost. Telemetry that robots could not deliver was buffered on the robots and uploaded after reconnection.

ROOT CAUSE

The direct cause was the change in v3.3.1 that failed to return timed out connections to the pool. The change had passed code review and all unit tests, because the tests used short lived pools and never ran long enough to exhaust one.

cases.question: How much advance warning does either side have to give when ending a job during the initial trial months?

retrieved.text:
Leaving the company
The probation period for new employees is 6 months. During probation either side may end the
employment with one month of notice. After probation, the notice period set in your contract
applies. Most contracts use two months.
Before the last day, your manager will agree a handover plan with you, and People Operations
will arrange an exit conversation. Access to systems is removed at the end of your last working
day. Employees who leave in good standing are welcome to stay in touch through the alumni
channel, and many former colleagues have returned to Lumen Robotics later in their careers.

The LR7 series is designed to meet the requirements of ISO 3691-4 for driverless industrial trucks. The safety functions are implemented on a separate controller that does not depend on the main computer. If the protective field of the safety scanner is violated, the robot performs a protective stop.
At full speed the LR7-X2 comes to a complete stop within 0.4 metres after a protective stop is triggered. The protective field adapts to the speed of the robot, and warning fields give pedestrians visible and audible notice before a stop becomes necessary. Each robot has four emergency stop buttons, one at each corner, which cut power to the drive motors.
Status is shown by a light ring around the top of the robot. Green means ready, blue means the robot is driving a mission, amber means that it is waiting or charging, and red means a fault. The light ring flashes when the identify command is received.
The robot emits an audible signal when it reverses, with a volume that is adjustable in the site settings. Integrators are responsible for the site risk assessment, including pedestrian separation and the handling of loads that are higher than the deck.

The LR7 series is designed for indoor use on flat, hard floors such as sealed concrete. The operating temperature range is 0 to 40 degrees Celsius, and the relative humidity must be between 10 and 90 percent without condensation. In cold storage environments a special variant is planned but is not part of this specification.
Storage temperature for robots with batteries removed is minus 20 to 50 degrees Celsius. The robots must not be used in explosive atmospheres, and they should be kept away from sources of strong electromagnetic interference such as large induction heaters.

Expenses
You may spend company money when it is necessary for your work, but you must be able to
show what it was spent on. Submit claims in the expense system within 30 days of the purchase.
Claims older than 30 days are only paid with the approval of the finance director.
A receipt is required for every expense above EUR 25. Below that amount, a short description is
enough. Receipts can be photographed and uploaded, and the original does not need to be kept
after the claim is paid.
While travelling, meals are reimbursed up to EUR 55 per day in total. Alcohol is not reimbursed,
except for a moderate amount at a client dinner that has been announced to the manager
beforehand. Team meals during a project workshop are reimbursed up to EUR 30 per person.
Approvals follow the size of the claim. Your manager approves claims up to EUR 500. Claims
above EUR 500 also need the approval of a director. Approved claims are paid in the next payroll
cycle, which runs on the 25th of each month. Claims approved after the 18th of the month are
normally paid in the following cycle.
Corporate cards are available to employees who travel regularly. A card statement must be
reconciled in the expense system by the 5th of the following month. Cash advances are not
offered.
Memberships, subscriptions and software are not expenses. Please request them through the IT
portal so that licences can be tracked, and so that security can review the supplier.

The LR7-X2 is powered by the battery pack LB-48-30. It is a lithium iron phosphate pack with a nominal voltage of 48 V and a capacity of 30 Ah, which corresponds to an energy content of 1,440 Wh. The pack weighs 11.4 kg and can be exchanged in under two minutes without tools. A spare pack is available as SKU 80-4830.
The LR7-S1 uses the smaller LB-36-20 pack with 36 V, 20 Ah and 720 Wh. This gives the S1 a typical runtime of 7 hours, compared with 9.5 hours for the X2 in a typical shift with an average load of 20 kg and a mix of driving and waiting.
Charging is done with the dock LD-300. At the dock, the LR7-X2 charges from 0 to 80 percent in 52 minutes, and a full charge to 100 percent takes 85 minutes. The robot connects to the dock automatically through contacts on its front plate. Opportunity charging for short periods during idle time is supported and does not harm the pack.
The battery management system protects the pack against deep discharge. By default, the robot drives to the nearest free dock when the charge falls to 20 percent. The cells are rated for 1,500 full charge cycles before the capacity falls to 80 percent of the original value. The pack should be stored at a charge of about 50 percent if it is not used for more than a month.
Battery packs are classified as dangerous goods when shipped. Follow the transport instructions on the label and use only approved packaging.

Vacation
Full time employees receive 27 working days of paid vacation per calendar year. The entitlement
accrues at 2.25 days per month, so an employee who joins in the middle of the year receives a
proportional share. Public holidays in the Netherlands are not counted against vacation days.
Requests are made in the HR portal. A request for three days or fewer needs only your
manager's approval and should be answered within two working days. A request for 10 working
days or more in a row must be submitted at least four weeks in advance, so that teams can plan
coverage. Managers cannot refuse a request without suggesting an alternative period.
You may carry over up to 5 unused vacation days into the next year. Carried over days expire on
31 March, and the portal sends a reminder in February. Days above the carry over limit are lost,
except where an absence made it impossible to take them, in which case People Operations will
extend the deadline.
Employees who leave the company are paid for unused vacation days in their final salary
payment. If an employee has taken more days than they accrued, the difference is deducted from
the same payment.
Between Christmas Day and New Year's Day the office is closed for a company wide shutdown.
The shutdown days are granted in addition to the vacation entitlement, so nobody has to spend
their own days on it. Operations and field service teams keep a skeleton rota during the shutdown
and receive extra time off in return.

The incident happened on a Saturday night, which is a period of moderate load. If the pool had been exhausted on a weekday afternoon, all regions would likely have been affected. The customer's inventory count was also scheduled to finish at 06:00, so most of the failed missions could be repeated before the weekday shift began.

CUSTOMER COMMUNICATION

The communications lead used three channels during the incident: the public status page, direct email to the technical contacts of affected organisations, and phone calls from account managers to the five largest customers in the region. The first status page message was short and stated only that dispatch was degraded in Rotterdam, because we did not yet know the cause. The second message, at 03:19, said that robots might appear offline and that customers should avoid restarting robots, since a restart would not help and would add load.

After the incident, each affected customer received a written summary within two working days. Customers who asked for details received a call from an engineer. Several customers asked whether their own integration could have limited the damage, and the answer was yes: clients that back off when they see E-4471 and that check the robot status before retrying put much less pressure on the service. This led to action item AI-6.

The support team also noted that many customers could not tell the difference between a robot that was offline because of a local Wi-Fi problem and a robot that was offline because of our dispatch service. We will add a field to the robot status that shows whether the connection to the fleet service or the connection to the robot is the problem.

ACTION ITEMS

AI-1: Fix the connection pool leak and add a regression test that runs the pool for the equivalent of seven days. Owner: Teodor Vance. Shipped as a hotfix in v3.3.2 on 2026-03-19.

Robots connect to the fleet service through dual band Wi-Fi 6. An optional LTE module, sold as SKU LM-4G, provides a fallback connection when the facility network is not available. Roaming between access points takes less than 150 ms when the access points are configured as described in the network guide.
The LR7-X2 requires firmware version v3.2.0 or later. The LR7-S1 requires v3.3.0 or later. Firmware is updated over the air from the fleet service, and a robot downloads an update while it charges and installs it only when it is idle at the dock. Rolling back to the previous firmware is possible during the first 7 days after an update.
Integrators use the Lumen Fleet API to create missions and to read telemetry. Direct access to the robot over the network is possible only for the commissioning engineer, using the service port on the rear panel.

The following accessories are available for the LR7 series. The lift tray LA-118, sold as SKU 90-1180, raises the load by up to 300 mm and is intended for transfers to shelves and workstations. It adds 14 kg to the weight of the robot, which reduces the usable payload by the same amount when the tray is fitted to the LR7-S1.
The roller conveyor top LA-204 moves cartons on and off the robot at conveyor stations. The tote guide LA-310 keeps standard 600 by 400 mm totes in position on the deck during acceleration. Other accessories include a warning beacon, reflective navigation markers and a mounting kit for custom load carriers.
All accessories are detected automatically through a connector on the deck, and the robot adjusts its speed limits and stopping distances to the accessory that is fitted.

Data is kept only as long as there is a business or legal reason. The following periods apply, counted from the date the record was created unless stated otherwise.

Robot telemetry that is visible to customers is retained for 400 days. Operational logs of the fleet service are retained for 13 months. Security logs from the monitoring platform are retained for 18 months, to support investigations that start long after an event.

Customer support tickets are retained for 7 years. Contracts and invoices are retained for 7 years after the end of the contract, in line with tax rules. Employee records are retained for 7 years after the employee leaves the company, and applications from candidates who were not hired are deleted after 6 months.

Daily backups of production databases are retained for 35 days. Email in company mailboxes is retained for 3 years and then deleted automatically. Visitor registrations at reception are deleted after 12 months.

When a customer closes an account, their data is deleted from production systems within 30 days. Copies in backups disappear as the backups expire. Customers can ask for a deletion confirmation, and the security team issues it after the deletion has been verified.

Deletion must be carried out with the approved procedures. Simply emptying a folder is not enough for Restricted data, and hardware that held Confidential or Restricted data is destroyed by a certified supplier, which provides a certificate.

cases.question: What did ticket INC-20260314-03 report?

retrieved.text:
At 02:17 the monitoring rule FLEET-LAT-HIGH fired, because the median dispatch latency had risen above 5 seconds. The alert was routed to the on-call engineer, who acknowledged it at 02:24 after a first automatic page went unanswered for seven minutes. The delay is discussed in the section on what went poorly.

At 02:31 the first customer ticket arrived, INC-20260314-03, reporting that robots in hall 2 were not picking up new missions. A second ticket, INC-20260314-09, followed at 02:38 from another site. Support linked both tickets to the main incident record.

At 02:41 the on-call engineer declared a SEV-1 and Imara Kessel took over as incident commander. Bram Oosterhoek joined as communications lead and posted the first status page update at 02:49.

At 02:58 the team observed that the number of robots reporting error E-4471 to customers was rising steadily, which means that robots were being treated as offline even though they were powered on and reachable. This ruled out a network problem and pointed at the dispatch service itself.

At 03:05 the connection pool metrics showed that the pool was at its limit of 512 connections, with 509 in use and none returning. A heap comparison with a healthy region confirmed the leak, and engineers traced it to the reconnect change in v3.3.1.

At 03:12 the team decided against a simple restart. A restart would have restored service within minutes, but it would also have destroyed the evidence of the leak and risked a repeat within a few days. The incident commander chose to take a heap dump first and then perform a rollback.

At 03:32 the rollback of the dispatch service to the previous build started. The robots themselves were not touched, because the defect was in the service and not in the robot firmware.

At 03:58 the new instances were healthy and the pool was at 40 connections. Robots began reconnecting in batches of 50 to avoid a thundering herd.

POSTMORTEM: FLEET DISPATCH OUTAGE OF 14 MARCH 2026
Primary ticket: INC-20260314-07
Severity: SEV-1
Status: Reviewed on 2026-03-26, action items tracked until 2026-05-15
Authors: Imara Kessel (incident commander), Teodor Vance (on-call engineer)

SUMMARY

On Saturday 14 March 2026 the fleet dispatch service stopped assigning work to robots in the Rotterdam region for 1 hour and 53 minutes. During this time 418 of the 1,260 robots in the region lost their connection to the fleet service and stood still, and 37 missions failed. No person was injured and no robot was damaged. The cause was a connection pool leak that had been introduced in firmware release v3.3.1 and that only became visible when a weekend inventory count raised the number of simultaneous missions above the usual weekday level.

This document describes what happened, how we responded, what worked and what did not, and which actions we will take. It follows the blameless format: it names roles and decisions, and it does not look for individuals to blame.

BACKGROUND

The dispatch service receives mission requests, chooses a robot and sends the first waypoints. Each regional deployment keeps a pool of connections to the robots' message broker. In release v3.3.1, shipped on 24 February 2026, a refactoring of the reconnect logic changed the way connections were returned to the pool after a timeout. Connections that timed out while a robot was switching access points were not returned, and the pool slowly shrank.

On normal weekdays the pool recovers because the service restarts every night during the 03:00 maintenance window. On weekends the nightly restart is skipped for the Rotterdam region to avoid interrupting the large Saturday night shift of our biggest customer. As a result the pool had been running for 6 days without a restart when the incident began.

TIMELINE

All times are in UTC.

Released 2026-05-12. This minor release raises limits and adds mission chaining.

- The maximum number of waypoints in a mission was raised from 128 to 256. Missions with more waypoints are rejected with E-4472 (LUM-4980).
- Added the follow_up field to POST /missions, which lets a mission start another one automatically when it completes. This makes it possible to split long routes (LUM-4991).
- Added a sandbox environment at sandbox.lumenrobotics.example with 12 virtual robots (LUM-5002).
- Speed zones can now be drawn directly in the customer console, instead of editing the facility map file. Changes take effect within one minute (LUM-5017).
- Idempotency keys are now supported for POST /missions and POST /webhooks. A key is remembered for 24 hours (LUM-5030).
- The webhook delivery log in the console shows the response code of each attempt, which makes it easier to debug failing endpoints (LUM-5044).

Upgrade note: clients that assumed a limit of 128 waypoints do not need to change, but they can now send longer routes.

Released 2026-03-19. This is a hotfix for the dispatch outage described in ticket INC-20260314-07.

- Fixed a connection pool leak in the dispatch service that was introduced in v3.3.1. Connections that time out while a robot switches access points are now returned to the pool (LUM-4851).
- Added a regression test that runs the pool for the equivalent of seven days (LUM-4852).
- Added a metric for connection pool occupancy to the monitoring dashboard (LUM-4853).
- Robots are now reconnected in batches of 50 after a service restart, to avoid overloading the dispatch service (LUM-4860).

Customers running v3.3.1 should update as soon as possible. No change is needed on the robots themselves, because the defect was in the service.

AI-2: Create an alert that fires when the pool usage stays above 80 percent for 15 minutes. Owner: Imara Kessel. Due 2026-03-27 and completed on 2026-03-26.

AI-3: Change the pager policy so that an unacknowledged page escalates to the secondary engineer after 3 minutes instead of 10. Owner: Bram Oosterhoek. Due 2026-03-31.

AI-4: Add an alert on the 99th percentile of dispatch latency, with a threshold of 2 seconds. Owner: Teodor Vance. Due 2026-04-10.

AI-5: Extend the load test environment with a soak test of 72 hours that runs before every release candidate. Owner: the release engineering team. Due 2026-05-15.

AI-6: Update the integration guides for customer systems to describe retry with backoff and the Retry-After header. Owner: the developer relations team. Due 2026-04-24.

LESSONS

Slow resource leaks are invisible to short tests, to median based alerts and to humans looking at dashboards once a week. The most effective countermeasure is an alert on the resource itself, together with a long running test that asks whether the system is healthy after days and not minutes.

We also learned that an incident process works best when the first ten minutes are boring. The delays of seven minutes and ten minutes in this incident came from a pager configuration and not from any difficulty in the technical work. The response after the declaration of the SEV-1 was fast and well coordinated.

This postmortem was reviewed in the engineering all hands meeting on 2026-03-26. Progress on the remaining action items is reported in the weekly reliability review until the last one is closed.

Systems are scanned for vulnerabilities every week, and the results are tracked in the ticket system. The target time for remediation depends on severity. Critical vulnerabilities must be fixed within 7 days, high severity vulnerabilities within 30 days and medium severity vulnerabilities within 90 days. Low severity findings are fixed during normal maintenance.

An external company performs a penetration test of the fleet service and the customer console once a year. The summary of the findings is shared with customers who ask for it under a confidentiality agreement. Researchers who find a vulnerability can report it to security@lumenrobotics.example. We acknowledge reports within 2 working days and do not take legal action against good faith research.

Robot firmware is signed with a Restricted key. The build pipeline refuses to publish an image that is not signed, and robots refuse to install one.

Everyone must report suspected security incidents immediately. Typical examples are phishing emails that were opened, lost devices, accidental disclosure of data and unusual activity on an account. A report is never held against the person who makes it.

The security team classifies incidents by severity and appoints an incident commander for each SEV-1 and SEV-2. If personal data of customers or employees is affected, the data protection officer decides whether regulators must be notified. Regulators are informed within 72 hours of the moment we become aware of a confirmed personal data breach, and affected customers are informed without undue delay.

After every SEV-1 a blameless postmortem is written within 10 working days. It lists the timeline, the causes and the actions, and the actions are tracked until they are closed.

A sandbox is available at https://sandbox.lumenrobotics.example/v2 for integration testing. It simulates a fleet of 12 virtual robots at a virtual site called Demo Hall. Virtual robots respond to commands within one second and never run low on battery unless you ask them to, which you can do by sending the special command drain with a target percentage. The sandbox enforces the same error codes as production, so you can provoke E-4471 by sending the command go_offline to a virtual robot.

Sandbox tokens are separate from production tokens and are valid for 24 hours. Data in the sandbox is reset every night at 03:00 UTC, so do not rely on missions or webhooks persisting across days. Rate limits in the sandbox are lower than in production, at 120 requests per minute.

Official client libraries exist for Python, TypeScript and Java. They handle token refresh, pagination and retry on rate limit responses automatically. If you write your own client, follow the same rules: refresh tokens a minute before they expire, treat a missing next_cursor as the end of a list, and never retry a command after receiving E-4471 without checking the robot status first.

The libraries expose the request_id of every failed call on the exception object, which makes it easy to attach to support tickets. They are released on the first Tuesday of each month, independently of firmware releases, and the changelog is part of each package.

Breaking changes are introduced only in a new major version, and the previous major version is supported for 12 months after the new one is released. Deprecations are announced by email to the technical contacts of the organisation and in the response header Deprecation. The status page at https://status.lumenrobotics.example shows current incidents, and enterprise customers can reach the support team around the clock at api-support@lumenrobotics.example.

The incident happened on a Saturday night, which is a period of moderate load. If the pool had been exhausted on a weekday afternoon, all regions would likely have been affected. The customer's inventory count was also scheduled to finish at 06:00, so most of the failed missions could be repeated before the weekday shift began.

CUSTOMER COMMUNICATION

The communications lead used three channels during the incident: the public status page, direct email to the technical contacts of affected organisations, and phone calls from account managers to the five largest customers in the region. The first status page message was short and stated only that dispatch was degraded in Rotterdam, because we did not yet know the cause. The second message, at 03:19, said that robots might appear offline and that customers should avoid restarting robots, since a restart would not help and would add load.

After the incident, each affected customer received a written summary within two working days. Customers who asked for details received a call from an engineer. Several customers asked whether their own integration could have limited the damage, and the answer was yes: clients that back off when they see E-4471 and that check the robot status before retrying put much less pressure on the service. This led to action item AI-6.

The support team also noted that many customers could not tell the difference between a robot that was offline because of a local Wi-Fi problem and a robot that was offline because of our dispatch service. We will add a field to the robot status that shows whether the connection to the fleet service or the connection to the robot is the problem.

ACTION ITEMS

AI-1: Fix the connection pool leak and add a regression test that runs the pool for the equivalent of seven days. Owner: Teodor Vance. Shipped as a hotfix in v3.3.2 on 2026-03-19.

Learning and development
Every employee has a personal learning budget of EUR 1,200 per year. It can be used for
courses, books, conferences and certifications related to your role or your career plans.
Conference tickets are paid from the budget, while the travel is paid by the team. Unused budget
does not carry over to the next year.
Employees are also entitled to 3 days of paid study leave per year for courses or exams. New
starters get a mentor from another team for their first six months, and the company runs a
quarterly internal talk series where anyone can present a project.
Performance conversations take place twice a year, in April and in October. They are about
growth and feedback, not about pay: salary reviews are handled separately in January.

This document specifies the Lumen LR7 series of autonomous mobile robots for warehouse intralogistics. It covers the two production models, the LR7-X2 and the LR7-S1, their mechanical dimensions, battery system, sensors, safety functions and software requirements. It is written for integrators, safety officers and facility planners. Commercial terms are handled separately by the sales team and are not part of this specification.

The LR7 series carries totes, cartons and small pallets between storage racks, packing stations and loading docks. The robots navigate without floor markings by combining a 360 degree lidar scanner, wheel odometry and a map of the facility that is built during commissioning. A fleet of up to 400 robots can be coordinated by one fleet service instance, and the robots are controlled through the Lumen Fleet API.
Two models share the same software and the same docking infrastructure. The LR7-X2 is the standard model for loads up to 40 kilograms and is sold under SKU 70-2210. The LR7-S1 is a compact model for narrow aisles and is sold under SKU 70-2105. Both are delivered with a safety scanner, a battery pack and a quick start kit.

The LR7-X2 measures 1,120 mm in length, 740 mm in width and 420 mm in height with the standard deck. Its unladen weight is 86 kg, including the battery pack. The deck surface is 1,000 mm long and 700 mm wide and sits 380 mm above the floor.
The LR7-S1 is smaller. It measures 860 mm in length, 560 mm in width and 360 mm in height, and its unladen weight is 52 kg. The deck of the S1 is 760 mm long and 520 mm wide. The S1 fits through aisles as narrow as 900 mm, while the X2 requires at least 1,300 mm for turning.
The rated payload is 40 kg for the LR7-X2 and 12 kg for the LR7-S1. The payload is the maximum mass on the deck, including any accessory that is mounted on it. The load should be centred within 100 mm of the middle of the deck to preserve the rated stopping distance.

Both models use a differential drive with two hub motors and two passive casters. The LR7-X2 has two 400 W hub motors and wheels of 200 mm diameter made of polyurethane. The maximum speed of the LR7-X2 is 2.2 metres per second when unladen and 1.5 metres per second at full payload. The robot accelerates at up to 0.8 metres per second squared.
The X2 can climb ramps with a gradient of up to 5 percent and cross floor gaps of up to 15 mm. Larger gaps and steps require a bridging plate. The turning radius is zero, because the robot can rotate on the spot. Positioning accuracy at a workstation is plus or minus 10 mm without a docking marker and plus or minus 3 mm with one.
The motion controller limits speed automatically when the robot carries a load higher than 30 kg, when it travels in a zone marked as pedestrian area, and when the floor friction estimate falls below the configured threshold. Speed zones are set in the facility map by the commissioning engineer.

Released 2025-11-20. This patch release fixes issues found in the first weeks of v3.2.0.

- Fixed a localisation drift in long corridors where the lidar saw no features. Robots now use wheel odometry with a higher weight in such sections (LUM-4310).
- Docking contacts are retried up to three times if the first connection fails, which removes most failed charging attempts (LUM-4322).
- Fixed a bug that caused webhook signatures to be computed over a re-serialised body instead of the raw body (LUM-4329).
- Reduced the size of firmware downloads by 35 percent through delta updates (LUM-4337).

Released 2025-11-04. This minor release is the first to support the LR7-X2 and the second major version of the API.

- Added support for the LR7-X2 robot. Firmware v3.2.0 is the oldest firmware that can run on the LR7-X2 (LUM-4101).
- API version 2 became generally available. Version 1 remains supported until 2026-11-04 (LUM-4120).
- Added webhooks with HMAC signatures, delivered with up to 6 retries (LUM-4144).
- Added the telemetry history endpoint with a resolution of ten seconds (LUM-4160).
- Added opportunity charging at the dock LD-300, so robots can top up during idle periods. A charge to 80 percent now takes 52 minutes (LUM-4175).
- The token lifetime was shortened from 24 hours to 3600 seconds. Clients must refresh tokens more often (LUM-4188).

Upgrade note: clients that cached tokens for a day will receive E-4003 after an hour and must request a new token.

Robots connect to the fleet service through dual band Wi-Fi 6. An optional LTE module, sold as SKU LM-4G, provides a fallback connection when the facility network is not available. Roaming between access points takes less than 150 ms when the access points are configured as described in the network guide.
The LR7-X2 requires firmware version v3.2.0 or later. The LR7-S1 requires v3.3.0 or later. Firmware is updated over the air from the fleet service, and a robot downloads an update while it charges and installs it only when it is idle at the dock. Rolling back to the previous firmware is possible during the first 7 days after an update.
Integrators use the Lumen Fleet API to create missions and to read telemetry. Direct access to the robot over the network is possible only for the commissioning engineer, using the service port on the rear panel.

The following accessories are available for the LR7 series. The lift tray LA-118, sold as SKU 90-1180, raises the load by up to 300 mm and is intended for transfers to shelves and workstations. It adds 14 kg to the weight of the robot, which reduces the usable payload by the same amount when the tray is fitted to the LR7-S1.
The roller conveyor top LA-204 moves cartons on and off the robot at conveyor stations. The tote guide LA-310 keeps standard 600 by 400 mm totes in position on the deck during acceleration. Other accessories include a warning beacon, reflective navigation markers and a mounting kit for custom load carriers.
All accessories are detected automatically through a connector on the deck, and the robot adjusts its speed limits and stopping distances to the accessory that is fitted.

The LR7-X2 is powered by the battery pack LB-48-30. It is a lithium iron phosphate pack with a nominal voltage of 48 V and a capacity of 30 Ah, which corresponds to an energy content of 1,440 Wh. The pack weighs 11.4 kg and can be exchanged in under two minutes without tools. A spare pack is available as SKU 80-4830.
The LR7-S1 uses the smaller LB-36-20 pack with 36 V, 20 Ah and 720 Wh. This gives the S1 a typical runtime of 7 hours, compared with 9.5 hours for the X2 in a typical shift with an average load of 20 kg and a mix of driving and waiting.
Charging is done with the dock LD-300. At the dock, the LR7-X2 charges from 0 to 80 percent in 52 minutes, and a full charge to 100 percent takes 85 minutes. The robot connects to the dock automatically through contacts on its front plate. Opportunity charging for short periods during idle time is supported and does not harm the pack.
The battery management system protects the pack against deep discharge. By default, the robot drives to the nearest free dock when the charge falls to 20 percent. The cells are rated for 1,500 full charge cycles before the capacity falls to 80 percent of the original value. The pack should be stored at a charge of about 50 percent if it is not used for more than a month.
Battery packs are classified as dangerous goods when shipped. Follow the transport instructions on the label and use only approved packaging.

The LR7 series is designed to meet the requirements of ISO 3691-4 for driverless industrial trucks. The safety functions are implemented on a separate controller that does not depend on the main computer. If the protective field of the safety scanner is violated, the robot performs a protective stop.
At full speed the LR7-X2 comes to a complete stop within 0.4 metres after a protective stop is triggered. The protective field adapts to the speed of the robot, and warning fields give pedestrians visible and audible notice before a stop becomes necessary. Each robot has four emergency stop buttons, one at each corner, which cut power to the drive motors.
Status is shown by a light ring around the top of the robot. Green means ready, blue means the robot is driving a mission, amber means that it is waiting or charging, and red means a fault. The light ring flashes when the identify command is received.
The robot emits an audible signal when it reverses, with a volume that is adjustable in the site settings. Integrators are responsible for the site risk assessment, including pedestrian separation and the handling of loads that are higher than the deck.

The LR7 series is designed for indoor use on flat, hard floors such as sealed concrete. The operating temperature range is 0 to 40 degrees Celsius, and the relative humidity must be between 10 and 90 percent without condensation. In cold storage environments a special variant is planned but is not part of this specification.
Storage temperature for robots with batteries removed is minus 20 to 50 degrees Celsius. The robots must not be used in explosive atmospheres, and they should be kept away from sources of strong electromagnetic interference such as large induction heaters.

The LR7-X2 runs on every release from v3.2.0 onwards. The LR7-S1 runs on every release from v3.3.0 onwards, because the smaller battery pack and the different drive controller needed new motion parameters. The lift tray LA-118 is supported from v3.3.0 on both models. Mixed fleets of both models are supported on any release that supports both.

The API features introduced in each release are cumulative. A client written against v3.2.0 keeps working on v3.4.1, with the exceptions listed in the upgrade notes above: shorter token lifetimes from v3.2.0, command and stream limits from v3.3.0, and the higher waypoint limit from v3.4.0, which only relaxes a restriction.

Security fixes are listed separately so that customers can prioritise upgrades. In v3.2.1 we closed an issue in which a debug port on the robot service panel stayed enabled after commissioning (LUM-4340). In v3.3.0 the signature check for firmware images was moved earlier in the installation process, so that an unsigned image is rejected before it is unpacked (LUM-4595). In v3.4.0 we added rate limiting for failed token requests, which stops password guessing against client secrets (LUM-5051).

No release in this range contains a fix for a vulnerability that was known to be exploited. Details of the severity rating are given in the security policy, which also describes how researchers can report problems.

Released 2026-02-24. This patch release refactors reconnect handling.

- Reconnect logic in the dispatch service was rewritten. The median time for a robot to reconnect after a Wi-Fi roam fell from 14 seconds to 6 seconds (LUM-4702).
- The default low battery threshold at which robots drive to the dock is now 20 percent, previously 25 percent. The setting can still be changed per site (LUM-4718).
- Fixed an issue where the identify command did not flash the status ring on robots that were charging (LUM-4725).
- The error message for E-4475 now includes the fault code of the robot.

Released 2026-01-27. This minor release adds a new robot model and tighter limits.

- Added support for the LR7-S1 compact robot. The LR7-S1 requires v3.3.0 or later (LUM-4501).
- Added support for the lift tray LA-118. Robots detect the tray automatically and adjust their speed limits (LUM-4533).
- Introduced a limit of 20 commands per minute per robot on POST /robots/{id}/commands. Requests above the limit are rejected with E-4290 (LUM-4560).
- Introduced the limit of 5 concurrent telemetry streams per organisation. The sixth stream returns E-4291 (LUM-4571).
- Geofences are now enforced when a mission is created, and a mission that leaves the geofence is rejected with E-5120 (LUM-4588).
- Telemetry history queries are limited to 24 hours per call.

Upgrade note: integrations that opened more than 5 telemetry streams must be changed before the upgrade, for example by selecting several robots in one stream.

stop, as long as you complete your contracted hours across the week. Please do not schedule

GET /telemetry/stream opens a server sent events stream with live data for the robots you select. Each event contains the robot id, position, speed, battery percentage and any active warnings. Requests are made through the access portal and approved by the system owner. Access to customer fleet data additionally requires approval by the head of customer operations.

Access rights are reviewed every quarter. Managers receive a list of the access rights of their team and must confirm or remove each one within 14 days. cases.question: What does error code E-4471 mean?

retrieved.text:
The following codes are returned in the code field of an error response. The HTTP status is given where it is fixed.

E-4003 means that the token has expired. The HTTP status is 401. Request a new token and repeat the call.

E-4030 means that the token lacks the required scope. The HTTP status is 403.

E-4409 means a mission conflict, as described in the section on missions. The HTTP status is 409.

E-4471 means that the target robot is offline. The HTTP status is 409.

E-4472 means that a mission has more than 256 waypoints. The HTTP status is 422.

E-4475 means that the robot is in the fault state and cannot accept the command. The HTTP status is 409.

E-4290 means that a rate limit was exceeded. The HTTP status is 429.

E-4291 means that the limit of concurrent telemetry streams was exceeded. The HTTP status is 429.

E-5012 means that the robot battery is too low to start the mission.

E-5120 means that the mission leaves the site geofence. The HTTP status is 422.

E-5301 means that the fleet service is temporarily unavailable. The HTTP status is 503. Retry with exponential backoff.

Codes beginning with E-4 indicate a problem with the request, and codes beginning with E-5 indicate a condition on the robot or in the service. Only E-5301 should be retried automatically without changing the request.

List endpoints are paginated. The default page size is 50 items and the maximum is 200 items, set with the limit query parameter. Responses include a next_cursor field. Pass its value as the cursor parameter to receive the next page. A missing next_cursor means that you have reached the end.

Requests that create resources accept an Idempotency-Key header. If you repeat a request with the same key within 24 hours, the server returns the original response instead of creating a second resource. Keys must be unique per organisation and at most 64 characters long.

All errors have the same shape: an object with the fields code, message and request_id. Please include the request_id when you contact support, because it lets us find the exact request in our logs.

GET /robots returns the robots in your fleet. Filter with the query parameters status, site and model. The status filter accepts online, offline, charging and fault.

GET /robots/{id} returns a single robot, including its model, firmware version, battery percentage and last known position. Robot ids look like rb_9f3k2m and never change during the life of a robot, even if it moves between sites.

POST /robots/{id}/commands sends a command to one robot. The supported commands are pause, resume, return_to_dock and identify. The identify command flashes the status ring for ten seconds so that operators can find the robot on the floor. Commands are queued for at most 30 seconds. If the robot does not acknowledge a command within this window, the call fails.

If the target robot is not connected to the fleet service, the command is rejected with error code E-4471 and HTTP status 409. This is the most common error in production. Before retrying, check the robot status with GET /robots/{id}. A robot that stays offline for more than five minutes also raises an alert in the customer console.

Commands to a robot in the fault state are rejected with error code E-4475, except for identify, which is always accepted.

At 02:17 the monitoring rule FLEET-LAT-HIGH fired, because the median dispatch latency had risen above 5 seconds. The alert was routed to the on-call engineer, who acknowledged it at 02:24 after a first automatic page went unanswered for seven minutes. The delay is discussed in the section on what went poorly.

At 02:31 the first customer ticket arrived, INC-20260314-03, reporting that robots in hall 2 were not picking up new missions. A second ticket, INC-20260314-09, followed at 02:38 from another site. Support linked both tickets to the main incident record.

At 02:41 the on-call engineer declared a SEV-1 and Imara Kessel took over as incident commander. Bram Oosterhoek joined as communications lead and posted the first status page update at 02:49.

At 02:58 the team observed that the number of robots reporting error E-4471 to customers was rising steadily, which means that robots were being treated as offline even though they were powered on and reachable. This ruled out a network problem and pointed at the dispatch service itself.

At 03:05 the connection pool metrics showed that the pool was at its limit of 512 connections, with 509 in use and none returning. A heap comparison with a healthy region confirmed the leak, and engineers traced it to the reconnect change in v3.3.1.

At 03:12 the team decided against a simple restart. A restart would have restored service within minutes, but it would also have destroyed the evidence of the leak and risked a repeat within a few days. The incident commander chose to take a heap dump first and then perform a rollback.

At 03:32 the rollback of the dispatch service to the previous build started. The robots themselves were not touched, because the defect was in the service and not in the robot firmware.

At 03:58 the new instances were healthy and the pool was at 40 connections. Robots began reconnecting in batches of 50 to avoid a thundering herd.

A sandbox is available at https://sandbox.lumenrobotics.example/v2 for integration testing. It simulates a fleet of 12 virtual robots at a virtual site called Demo Hall. Virtual robots respond to commands within one second and never run low on battery unless you ask them to, which you can do by sending the special command drain with a target percentage. The sandbox enforces the same error codes as production, so you can provoke E-4471 by sending the command go_offline to a virtual robot.

Sandbox tokens are separate from production tokens and are valid for 24 hours. Data in the sandbox is reset every night at 03:00 UTC, so do not rely on missions or webhooks persisting across days. Rate limits in the sandbox are lower than in production, at 120 requests per minute.

Official client libraries exist for Python, TypeScript and Java. They handle token refresh, pagination and retry on rate limit responses automatically. If you write your own client, follow the same rules: refresh tokens a minute before they expire, treat a missing next_cursor as the end of a list, and never retry a command after receiving E-4471 without checking the robot status first.

The libraries expose the request_id of every failed call on the exception object, which makes it easy to attach to support tickets. They are released on the first Tuesday of each month, independently of firmware releases, and the changelog is part of each package.

Breaking changes are introduced only in a new major version, and the previous major version is supported for 12 months after the new one is released. Deprecations are announced by email to the technical contacts of the organisation and in the response header Deprecation. The status page at https://status.lumenrobotics.example shows current incidents, and enterprise customers can reach the support team around the clock at api-support@lumenrobotics.example.

The API reference was reorganised in v3.4.0. Error codes now have their own section, with the HTTP status listed next to each code where it is fixed. The product specification of the LR7 series was updated in v3.3.0 to describe the LR7-S1. We also added worked examples for webhook signature verification in Python, TypeScript and Java to the client libraries, and a troubleshooting page that explains the most common errors, starting with E-4471.

Customers who maintain internal runbooks for their operators should review the pages on robot states, because the status values charging and fault were clarified in v3.3.1. A robot that is charging can accept all commands, while a robot in the fault state accepts only identify.

Upgrade one minor version at a time on production sites, and test each step in the sandbox first. Skipping a minor version is supported, but then the upgrade notes of all skipped versions apply together. If you manage more than 100 robots, schedule the rollout in waves, so that no more than 25 percent of the fleet installs an update at the same time. Robots that miss an update window install it at the next idle period.

For customers on long term support contracts, the platform team publishes a compatibility matrix with every release. The matrix shows which robot models run on which firmware versions and which API features each version offers. A short summary is printed at the start of each release note, and the full matrix is in the customer console under Fleet settings.

Downgrades are possible for 7 days after an update for robots, but not for cloud services. If you need to roll back after that period, contact support. Rollbacks of the dispatch service are performed by Lumen engineers and are described in the internal runbook.

A mission is an ordered list of waypoints that a robot drives and a set of actions at each waypoint, such as lifting or lowering a tray.

POST /missions creates a mission and assigns it to a robot or to the fleet. The request body contains a name, an optional robot_id, a priority from 1 to 5 and a list of waypoints. Priority 5 missions preempt lower priority missions. A mission may contain at most 256 waypoints. A body that exceeds this limit is rejected with error code E-4472 and HTTP status 422. Split long routes into several missions that are chained with the follow_up field.

GET /missions lists missions, newest first, and supports the filters state and robot_id. The state of a mission is one of queued, running, paused, completed, failed or cancelled.

DELETE /missions/{id} cancels a queued or running mission. A running mission stops at its next safe point, which is normally within two seconds. Completed missions cannot be deleted, and an attempt returns error code E-4409 with HTTP status 409. The same code is returned when a new mission conflicts with a mission that is already running on the same robot and has the same or higher priority.

If a robot has less than 15 percent charge when a mission is about to start, the mission is not started and the call fails with error code E-5012. Missions are re-queued automatically after the robot has returned to the dock and charged above 30 percent. Operators can override this behaviour in the site settings, but we advise against it.

A mission that leaves the geofence configured for its site is rejected at creation with error code E-5120. Geofences are managed in the customer console, and changes become effective within one minute.

At 04:10 all 418 affected robots had reconnected and the dispatch latency was back to its normal median of 0.4 seconds. The incident commander declared the service restored. The total duration from the first alert to restoration was 1 hour and 53 minutes.

At 04:35 the status page was updated to resolved and the customer in Rotterdam received a direct call from the account manager. Monitoring stayed in heightened mode until 08:00.

IMPACT

The outage affected only the Rotterdam region. Of the 1,260 robots deployed there, 418 lost their connection, which is about 33 percent. The remaining robots continued to execute missions that were already assigned to them, but they did not receive new work, so they went idle once their queue was empty.

In total, 37 missions failed and had to be re-created by the customer. A further 112 missions were delayed by more than 30 minutes. Customers received no financial penalties from us automatically, and the commercial follow up was handled by the account team outside of this document.

The most visible technical symptom for integrators was a flood of rejected commands with error E-4471. The peak was 6,300 rejected commands per minute at 03:20. Some customer clients retried aggressively and added load, which delayed reconnection for a few minutes. Several customers also hit the rate limit and received E-4290.

No data was lost. Telemetry that robots could not deliver was buffered on the robots and uploaded after reconnection.

ROOT CAUSE

The direct cause was the change in v3.3.1 that failed to return timed out connections to the pool. The change had passed code review and all unit tests, because the tests used short lived pools and never ran long enough to exhaust one.

The LR7 series is designed to meet the requirements of ISO 3691-4 for driverless industrial trucks. The safety functions are implemented on a separate controller that does not depend on the main computer. If the protective field of the safety scanner is violated, the robot performs a protective stop.
At full speed the LR7-X2 comes to a complete stop within 0.4 metres after a protective stop is triggered. The protective field adapts to the speed of the robot, and warning fields give pedestrians visible and audible notice before a stop becomes necessary. Each robot has four emergency stop buttons, one at each corner, which cut power to the drive motors.
Status is shown by a light ring around the top of the robot. Green means ready, blue means the robot is driving a mission, amber means that it is waiting or charging, and red means a fault. The light ring flashes when the identify command is received.
The robot emits an audible signal when it reverses, with a volume that is adjustable in the site settings. Integrators are responsible for the site risk assessment, including pedestrian separation and the handling of loads that are higher than the deck.

The LR7 series is designed for indoor use on flat, hard floors such as sealed concrete. The operating temperature range is 0 to 40 degrees Celsius, and the relative humidity must be between 10 and 90 percent without condensation. In cold storage environments a special variant is planned but is not part of this specification.
Storage temperature for robots with batteries removed is minus 20 to 50 degrees Celsius. The robots must not be used in explosive atmospheres, and they should be kept away from sources of strong electromagnetic interference such as large induction heaters.

cases.question: What is the recommended safeguard against problems that build up slowly over days?
